en: *Daṇḍa-śāstra*, one fascicle.
Composed by the Venerable Śākyaprabha;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
There are certain beings in the world who, lacking wisdom and understanding, give rise to false attachments; out of compassion for those who thus sink into ruin, I have now composed this treatise.
The verse says:
Even on a level path, If one stumbles at every step,
For the sake of those who are ignorant and deluded, I shall discourse upon this Treatise on the Staff.
The treatise says:
Each and every World-Honored One appears in the world and then brings immeasurable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
However, all sentient beings have no end, for they are like space, being infinite by nature.
This is the principle set forth by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
"Limit" (*anta*) refers to the demarcation of a specific quantity;
since this is one [of the meanings], it is said "without limit" (*ananta*) to preclude that.

As for what is called "end" (*paryavasāna*), it means the sense of exhaustion or finality; because of this, there is no fault of the inseparability between the thesis (*sādhya*) and the proof (*sādhana*).
To claim that the thesis (pakṣa) has no end and the reason (hetu) is boundless is a fault of partiality within the thesis itself.
A proponent of a divergent view states this:
"We admit the existence of newly born sentient beings who have never existed before, just as in the case of a village of spirits."
As their calculation goes: although forests and thickets undergo great expense through felling and the like, they are seen to grow anew once they have been destroyed;

because the cause is inexhaustible, it must therefore be admitted that there are distinct sentient beings who have newly arisen where none existed before—this is a brief explanation of their argument.
As it is stated in the *Saṃkṣiptavyākhyāna* (Brief Exposition), in response to a question, he addressed the army of physicians, saying:
"There are sentient beings who are ancient, and there are sentient beings who are new," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, one must certainly grant this:

if it were otherwise, then just as a heap of sesame seeds and the like—without any new additions—is seen to reach its end through depletion, so too [the continuum] would necessarily be seen to have a final exhaustion.
If there were such a thing as a sentient being who had never existed before and only now newly arises, it would follow that one accepts that birth and death have a beginning.
If one accepts a beginning, then there is the fault of [existence] being without a cause.
Since you have admitted that there is no cause, it would follow that everything exists without a cause;
this is the fundamental intention of the Ācārya.
To this, he further provides the following reply:

Because there exists karma that establishes a connection within the offspring—namely, the seeds of both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas—the ādāna-vijñāna, the kalala, and so forth arise for the very first time.

Once one has become attached, by virtue of the good or evil karma one has personally created through proximity [to objects], one enters into the cycle of transmigration or emerges into nirvāṇa; this is precisely the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), namely *saṃskāra-aṣṭika* and *vijñāna-āpa-bhava-aṣṭika*.
Since this principle already exists within your own school, how can you insist on asserting that there are newly born sentient beings?
By doing so, you would incur the fallacy that birth and death have a beginning.
Another proponent says:
This is not a refined answer. Why is that?
If there were the possibility of new arising, then there would be an increase or surplus.
Since increase depends upon decrease, the former [the beginning] would be without cause.

If it is argued that these newly arisen sentient beings were previously unaware of the purpose of birth and death, and were suddenly born solely through the power of conditions consisting of the karma of others; [this is untenable].
If this were the case, those sentient beings currently undergoing transmigration would, in each and every moment, arise from one another in such a way as to become redundant.

By this reasoning, the proponents of the theory of new birth (navotpāda-vāda) must admit that there was originally a first sentient being; for since they admit an increase [in population], which depends upon a prior decrease, they must admit that at all times there is the new birth of numerous sentient beings.
These various mental factors (caitta) are certain to increase, because each preceding moment depends upon their subsequent decrease.
If this is the case, they are able to decrease until they become fewer and fewer, until at the point of death, only a single one remains.
However, this initial [moment] becomes "initial" without depending on any other karma; thus, it would be an existence without a cause, which certainly cannot avoid the fault of being uncaused.
If one were to say that there must necessarily be an addition [of a cause], then this fault could be incurred.
That which increases without being consumed is a cause for surplus, such as the property of a miserly person.
However, there is a principle according to which sentient beings undergo diminution. Why is this so?
It is not as if each and every Buddha, through *upādāna*, leads countless sentient beings into *parinirvāṇa* in such a manner.
The verse says:
Because the appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter, faith in his teaching is likewise hard to find.
Since the causes for birth are easily found, yet the principle of liberation is of a different nature.
The treatise says:
Because the appearance of a Buddha in the world is truly difficult to encounter, as it is stated in the treatise:

During the first incalculable eon, he had already served five times seventy thousand Buddhas; during the second, six times seventy thousand Buddhas; and during the third, seven times seventy thousand Buddhas.
Because the provisions for attaining Buddhahood are extremely difficult to obtain, as a verse says:
"Through countless hundreds of ascetic practices, Countless roots of goodness have been produced."
Advancing through countless long eons, severing countless afflictive obstructions,
one attains all-encompassing wisdom; having purified all hindrances and disturbances,
one becomes the Unsurpassed World-Honored One, like opening a casket to behold its treasures.

"Even granting that one might occasionally encounter the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world, those who possess sincere faith and reverence for the pure Dharma and Vinaya he proclaims are truly difficult to find; for such faith can only be fully realized within the eight states of leisure, yet these states themselves are of the most rare nature."

However, the causes for the arising [of existence] are extremely easy to obtain, namely afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma; this is because these causal conditions manifest frequently at almost any time.

These afflictions have three types of conditions: first, the non-abandonment of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); second, the manifestation of the objects of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); and third, the arising of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) toward them—this being what the foolish and ignorant mostly delight in and cling to.
Nevertheless, since all karmas merely arise through the attachment of their creators, the causes are not difficult to find; thus, it may be possible at some time to attain liberation.
To attempt to answer those new objections with such a meager expenditure of effort would certainly fail to avoid falling into error, as it is logically inconsistent.
The verse says:
The receptacle world has no time of increase; it contains the period of formation and the period of decrease.
Since birth and death have no beginning, this [world] ought to become greatly congested.
The treatise says:

If there were room for new [beings] to arise, they would continue to flow forth; however, this is because it is a world that is not a vessel [for sentient beings], unlike the world of sentient beings where there is the principle of increase.
Regarding the fixed number of worlds arranged horizontally and vertically, there may be times when they decrease, such as during the dissolution of a kalpa, because some realms become empty.
As it is said: "It is like the falling of rain from the sky; if Īśvara were to cause it, it would pour down from the sky without interval or deficiency."
In this way, in the eastern direction, there are worlds without interval or gap, some forming and others dissolving;
yet, there is no limit to the number of sentient beings newly born or newly growing therein.
However, since *sattvas* are so numerous as to be infinite, they cannot logically coexist; would they not then mutually oppress one another and undergo the suffering of confinement?

Now, let us further pose a question to the proponents of the theory of new birth (*abhinavotpāda-vādin*): when you assert that a previously non-existent sentient being suddenly arises, and consciousness is produced by relying on the power of other karmic forces—is this [consciousness] perfumed (*vāsita*) or unperfumed?

If one says that perfuming occurs from what is newly produced through attachment, then consciousness would become the substance of that perfuming; this gives rise to the faults of being both one and many.

Generally speaking, for perfuming to occur, it must involve the simultaneous arising and ceasing of both defiled and purified phenomena, such that, based upon this, they act as the cause for the production of those [phenomena].

Is it not the case that those sentient beings previously possessed a cause of arising such that those two dharmas could arise and cease together, and by depending upon this [cause], it acted as the cause for their arising?

However, that which is capable of being the point of attachment—consciousness—arises and ceases simultaneously with the preceding two dharmas and serves as the cause for their arising; in this, there is no contradiction or error whatsoever.

If that is so, and you admit that the initial consciousness is perfumed, then since its subsequent moments are attached in the same manner as the preceding moment—being its cause—the subsequent moments should likewise be so.
If it were otherwise, the principle of the dharma of perfuming (vāsanā) would not be established.
By this reasoning, if a father attains liberation through exertion or becomes learned through much hearing, his son should likewise attain it without exerting effort, just like his father.
At times it is like a son, and the father should likewise be so.
In such cases, many faults would arise, all of which would be incurred.
If one claims that [the result] does not arise from perfuming, yet various functional capacities arise spontaneously, [this is untenable].
If one attempts to defend this by saying:
"Because there is neither defilement nor purity, as they are identical in their arising and ceasing;
therefore, taking that as a cause entails the same fault as mentioned before."
Now, we merely take that which is capable of being attached; because causes and conditions conjoin, they act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that which lacks a root to arise.
This interpretation certainly avoids the fault of a result not being produced.
If that is so, then the capacity and its fruit perish, just like the capacity of karma.

Once the capacity belonging to those [defilements] such as greed has fulfilled its fruit, it ceases entirely; this is just as the capacity inherent in a ripening (vipāka) karma, having produced its fruit, immediately perishes.
If it were otherwise, it would result in the fault of being inexhaustible;
this case is likewise so. Even if that were the case, what loss would there be?
Because it is not permitted for other seeds to be cast [into the stream] for the sake of liberation, there is no need for further exertion.

Once the afflictions such as greed have been extinguished, these very afflictions are abandoned; with respect to their respective fruits, one no longer permits the casting of new seeds. Since the seeds are severed, even if one does not cultivate the Noble Path, one immediately attains parinirvāṇa.
This accords with the words of the deva Sudarśana, who, though speaking from his own private perspective, praised what is not the Dharma. As he said:
"I observe the multitudes of beings, With turbid minds and turbid bodies."
Abandoning all desires for worldly pleasures, one seeks elsewhere for the cause of ending suffering;
yet if one merely indulges in sublime bliss, why labor over other views?
By employing this very mind of greedy attachment, one immediately realizes the principle of Nirvana.
Furthermore, this leads to further faults because karma would then be rendered useless.
As it is briefly explained:
there are three types of meritorious actions, namely those consisting of giving (*dāna*), those consisting of ethical discipline (*śīla*), and those consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Is it truly useless to initiate diligent cultivation in this regard?
Why is this so? Because the fruit arises spontaneously through the power of the combination [of conditions].

When various meritorious deeds are about to perish, they deposit a maturation-impregnation (*vipāka-vāsanā*) within the *ālaya-vijñāna*; later, this impregnation, according to its own function, obtains an auxiliary cause for production and, through conjunction, brings about the future maturation that is to arise.
Thus, the diligent effort you have exerted in cultivating those meritorious deeds will not be in vain.

However, if one has not cultivated virtuous karma in the past, yet the potential for maturation (*vipāka*) suddenly arises by virtue of those current conditions as its causal link, then from this point on, the diligent cultivation [of merit]—just as before—will be useless for producing the body of suffering that constitutes the maturation of future existence within the present life.
Furthermore, the two types of karma—volition (*cetanā*) and what is produced by volition (*cetayitvā*), as well as the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral—would all become mere empty constructs.

If it is argued that there is subsequent perfuming (*vāsanā*), and that from the moment immediately following [the initial state], until adverse conditions arise, greed and other afflictions perfume one's own continuum, this would exclude the very first moment of the *ādānavijñāna*.
In this way, there will be no grounds for charging [the opponent] with various fallacies.
If this is the case, then the same applies to prior perfuming (*vāsanā*): by means of its own perfuming, it likewise becomes entirely exhausted and stale.
If it were not so, how could it serve as the generative cause for that [wisdom]?

Although supramundane wisdom has never been attained before, because it exists within one's own continuum, the wisdom that resembles the teaching of the two kinds of selflessness is universally accepted as serving as the generative cause from the place where this perfuming occurs.
This permeation by hearing is supremely pure, because its essential nature is the outflow of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The dharma-realm is the realization of the non-existence of both self and phenomena within the Tathāgata’s dharma-body; that which flows forth from this dharma-realm as its fruit is called the dharma-body.
The "element" (*dhātu*) is precisely the cause; it is the element of all supramundane phenomena because it can sustain their perfumed nature.
Furthermore, when the remaining habitual tendencies of both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions have been severed, it is called "utterly pure."
This perfuming by hearing resembles that fruit because it arises with that [fruit] as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and shares its essential nature (*svabhāva*). As it is said:

"The seeds of the perfuming by correct hearing possessed by all Bodhisattvas who have first resolved for enlightenment, though they are called 'worldly,' should be known as being subsumed within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); Śrāvaka, Boddhika, and Buddha should be known as being subsumed within the Liberation-body (*vimuktikāya*)."
Therefore, it is certain that although these are worldly, they can directly serve as the seeds for supramundane minds.

The meaning of the teaching resembles the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of consciousness; though it appears to be non-existent, by following its chapters and relying on the meaning of its phrases, one reveals the underlying principles of their mutual connection. This is demonstrated through a single section as a model, and all other verses are likewise the same.
Regarding this section on abandonment, although there are no distinct divisions for the sake of clarification, what fault would there be [in their absence]?
This would merely constitute a restatement; as it is in the subsequent part, it was likewise so in the preceding one.
However, it falls within one's own continuum and is perfumed by greed and the like.
If this is the case, then it arises from previously existing seeds; those [seeds] again from what preceded them, and those in turn from what preceded them still further.
Thus, all *sarvajña* (omniscient ones) arise from the seeds of the past; that which is grasped as newly arisen becomes the "unmanifested" (*asaṃskṛta*).
Based on this, one can establish the existence of prior lives.
Devadatta’s initial visual consciousness must necessarily arise from a preceding consciousness;
this should be known because its nature is that of consciousness, just like a subsequent consciousness.
Even if it were to arise from the attainment of cessation, the mind would still be included therein.
Within our own school, by means of rationality, there is likewise no fault of indefiniteness.
All mental states and mental factors are universally admitted to arise from four conditions;
yet you posit a "first" mind—what, then, could its equal-and-immediate condition be?
The principle established by the Abhidharma is definitive: mental states and mental factors arise from four conditions.
If that is so, regarding the initial arising of the mind which you accept, what serves as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

Nor does it exist within another continuum, because it is logically untenable for a collection of minds belonging to one continuum to serve as the conditions for a collection of one's own mind when their respective degrees of magnitude differ; furthermore, there is a fixed principle [to this effect].

According to your theory that all births are defiled by the afflictions of their own level, the defiled mind you admit exists at birth would not, in fact, be defiled by the afflictions of its own level.
Even with respect to objects in the three periods of time, the principle of birth-defilement cannot be established.
Furthermore, it is not of the past, because that has not been experienced;
nor is it of the future, because one forms a wish based on what was previously experienced;
nor is it of the present, because it arises through the sovereignty of the mental consciousness.
For it would then follow that [the self] is non-existent, deaf, blind, and so forth.

Furthermore, since the five sense faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of all realms of existence are all results of maturation (*vipāka*), your [self] would consequently not be a result of maturation.

The Venerable Kṣemadatta was exceptionally skilled in discourse on the sūtras; however, he stated that because the five internal bases are matured and nurtured, one knows that the five faculties, such as the eye, are of the nature of maturation (vipāka), and that the formation of the five destinies is likewise the essential nature of maturation. This is explained in brief for the sake of establishing the measure [of the argument].

Some say that because the venerable ones in the various hells experience the power of manifest outflows and afflictions, they consequently perform actions that lead to rebirth in hell, causing their lifespan there to increase.

This refers to the crooked, defiled, and turbid karma of body, speech, and mind; at the end of life, it causes the ripening of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to undergo extreme boiling in a loathsome and contemptible place.
Once it has arisen as a maturation (*vipākaja*), it is designated as a "Nāraka, venerable one.
Apart from those phenomena, no separate Nāraka can be found.
What are called "those phenomena" are precisely the meaning of the *saṃskāra* (constituent) that arises as a maturation.

The term "collection" (*rāśi*) used here is not without distinction; this meaning is precisely the negation of a real self that wanders through the various realms of existence. This principle should be understood accordingly: the intention is merely to encompass distinct collections.

Regarding what is called "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*): although the designation and substance of "sentient beings" (*sattva*) do not differ, in order to clarify those who possess maturation, it is said that within the five aggregates, the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral are not of the nature of a destiny (*gati*), nor are they the matured retribution itself.

If that [state] were also the essence of a destiny (gati), then one who has currently committed or frequently increased various unwholesome karmas leading to rebirth in hell would have to be called a "hell-being" (naraka) right now.

The essential nature of these various consciousnesses that constitute the continuum is exclusively non-obscured and neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta); it is called "sentient being" (sattva), and this is likewise stated in the *Abhidharma*.
Furthermore, it says:
"The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is *vipāka*. Upon careful analysis, the life-faculty is necessarily and exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).

This is because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* establishes that all dharmas are the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), for there has never been a single dharma that transcends the nature of maturation.
However, for you who propose a new theory of sentient beings, it follows that the faculties and so forth would not be *vipāka* (maturation).

This is because the various karmas for which those newly arisen sentient beings experience subsequent feelings did not exist previously, and karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) could not possibly exist at that time.
Because [the cause] is absent due to its excellence and other such factors, it would also follow that one could perform actions for others to bring about retribution for them.
Thus, those who are remarkably eloquent in discussing the sūtras employ this as a jest.
The *Hand-Stick Treatise* (Hastavālaprakaraṇa), one fascicle, which seeks to expound upon unwholesome sūtras and śāstras according to the author’s own personal views,
thereby contradicting the Āgamas.
